name: Pyrilutamide
lead: Pyrilutamide, developmental code KX-826, is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor antagonist designed for topical use in androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss) and acne. It is being developed by Suzhou Kintor Pharmaceuticals.[1][2] Wikipedia describes it as a high-affinity, selective silent antagonist of the androgen receptor.[1]

For appearance, the draw is hair retention and regrowth. Androgenetic alopecia is driven by dihydrotestosterone acting on follicles, and pyrilutamide is meant to block that signal in the scalp itself, aiming to avoid the systemic effects of oral antiandrogens and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.[2][5][6] The same mechanism in skin is being tested for acne by reducing androgen-driven sebum production.[2]

As of early 2025 Wikipedia lists it in phase 3 trials for hair loss and phase 2 for acne, and it has not been approved as a drug by a major regulator.[1] According to Grokipedia, a phase 3 trial in Chinese men met its primary endpoint versus baseline but not versus placebo, and cosmetic formulations were launched in China in July 2024.[2] In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums it is grouped with RU58841 as an experimental topical anti-androgen, and some users describe obtaining it outside regulated channels.[3][4][10]

paras: For hair, the pitch is regrowth and retention at the hairline and crown: scalp-applied antiandrogens aim to stop dihydrotestosterone from shrinking follicles, so thinning areas look fuller over time, without the whole-body effects that people associate with oral antiandrogens and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.[2][5][6] For acne, the same mechanism is aimed at androgen-driven oil production, which affects shine, breakouts and skin texture.[1][2]

The compound is investigated for androgenetic alopecia in men and women and for acne vulgaris. A diabetic foot ulcer programme was discontinued.[1] Topical antiandrogens are positioned in review literature as candidates that could avoid the systemic effects of oral antiandrogens and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.[5][6] Clascoterone, a topical antiandrogen already approved for acne, is the nearest comparator, according to Grokipedia.[2]

Pyrilutamide competes with dihydrotestosterone for the androgen receptor, blocking the signalling that drives follicular miniaturisation and sebaceous gland activity.[1][2] Because it is a silent antagonist, it binds the receptor without activating it.[1] Preclinical reports describe it as optimised from antiandrogen chemistry related to enzalutamide for skin delivery and rapid local metabolism, with low blood levels after topical application.[2]

Grokipedia reports in vitro AR binding and mouse hair-growth studies in which topical KX-826 promoted hair regrowth, and minipig toxicology with large safety margins over exposures linked to efficacy.[2] A 2026 medicinal chemistry paper used pyrilutamide as a benchmark for new topical 'soft drug' antagonists designed to be rapidly inactivated if absorbed, reporting comparable efficacy in a mouse hair-growth model.[9]

Wikipedia gives pyrilutamide the formula C21H15F5N4O2S, a molar mass of 482.43 g/mol, and a Canadian patent (CA 2829322) published in 2012 and issued in 2017 and assigned to Kintor.[1] Its potency against the androgen receptor is listed as an IC50 of 0.28 nM, compared with 3.1 nM for bicalutamide in the same table.[1] Wikipedia groups it with other nonsteroidal antiandrogens, a family that also includes RU-58841 and, as a topical antagonist for acne, clascoterone.[1]

Trial adverse events are reported as mild and mostly local, such as redness, itching or dryness.[2] Long-term human data are limited. A forum user on T Nation described experiencing unusual side effects after roughly three weeks of use and asked for guidance on recovery, an individual report that has not been verified.[4]

Suzhou Kintor Pharmaceuticals developed KX-826 in China. First-in-human phase 1 studies began in 2019 and 2020, followed by phase 2 studies in Chinese women and US men and a registrational phase 3 study in Chinese men, according to Grokipedia.[2][7][8] Cosmetic formulations launched in China in 2024 while pharmaceutical development continued, and a higher concentration and a combination with minoxidil have been tested in later studies.[2] Looksmax.org users began discussing the phase 2 results and online availability in threads on the topic.[10]

Wikipedia lists development for diabetic foot ulcers as discontinued, and as of February 2025 describes phase 3 for androgenetic alopecia and phase 2 for acne.[1] Because trial results have been released mainly through company statements, the sequence from phase 2 to the Chinese phase 3 is documented in secondary summaries, and peer-reviewed full reports are limited.[2]

RU-58841 is the compound most often mentioned alongside pyrilutamide in forums; it is a research chemical that has not completed human drug development, and the two are discussed as experimental topical antiandrogens with the same rationale of blocking the androgen receptor locally.[3][1] Clascoterone is the topical antiandrogen that regulators have approved for acne, and Grokipedia treats it as the nearest comparator for pyrilutamide's acne program.[2]

Oral options for hair loss, finasteride and dutasteride, work by lowering DHT production, while a topical receptor blocker acts at the follicle instead; review articles on emerging therapies place topical antiandrogens among the strategies under study for male pattern hair loss.[5][6]

Two phase 1 studies registered on ClinicalTrials.gov tested single and multiple ascending topical doses of KX-826 in 40 men with androgenetic alopecia each, with safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics as the aims.[7][8] Grokipedia reports that adverse events were mostly mild application-site reactions with minimal systemic exposure.[2]

Per Grokipedia, a Chinese phase 2 study in women reported a target-area hair count increase of 11.39 hairs per cm2 versus placebo at 24 weeks, and a US phase 2 study in men reported a 15.34 hairs per cm2 increase from baseline at 24 weeks, with positive trends versus placebo.[2] The same source reports that the registrational Chinese phase 3 trial in men met its endpoint versus baseline but did not reach statistical significance versus placebo, that a 52-week extension showed sustained hair count and width signals, and that a higher-concentration study and a combination with minoxidil have reported results.[2] These results are drawn from company announcements summarised by a non-peer-reviewed encyclopedia, and peer-reviewed full reports are limited. Reviews of emerging hair-loss therapies list topical antiandrogens among candidates.[5][6]

No head-to-head trial of pyrilutamide against minoxidil or finasteride has been published, and company-reported combination studies with minoxidil are described only in summary form.[2] The phase 1 trials registered the primary outcomes as safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics rather than hair counts.[7][8]

Discussion is concentrated on looksmax.org and T Nation. A looksmax.org thread shared a blog summary of the phase 2 results, with posters noting they appeared comparable to oral finasteride in the summary and that people were already ordering the compound online before trials finished.[10] A T Nation poster lists it with RU-58841 as a topical anti-androgen that is not FDA approved and that, like other hair treatments, must be continued to maintain results.[3]

lore.intro: Community material on pyrilutamide is sparse. It appears as brief mentions on T Nation alongside RU58841 and in a looksmax.org thread about phase 2 results.[3][4][10]

claims.claim: Pyrilutamide is a topical anti-androgen that works like RU58841 for hair
claims.believers: A T Nation poster lists it with RU-58841 as topical anti-androgens that work, noting they are not FDA approved and must be maintained [3].
claims.experts: Company-reported phase 2 data show hair count gains, while the phase 3 trial in Chinese men reportedly did not separate from placebo; no published comparison with RU58841 exists [2].

claims.claim: A topical anti-androgen cannot cause systemic side effects
claims.believers: Proponents point to its design for rapid local metabolism as limiting systemic action [2].
claims.experts: Early trials reported minimal plasma levels and mild adverse events, but one forum user reported unusual symptoms after short use, and long-term data are limited [2][4].

claims.claim: The phase 2 data are 'comparable to oral finasteride' and it can be stacked with finasteride
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster summarising a blog write-up of the phase 2 results said they looked comparable to oral finasteride with itching the main side effect, and that because it acts at the follicle rather than blocking DHT production it could be combined with finasteride.[10]
claims.experts: No head-to-head trial of pyrilutamide and finasteride has been published, and the phase 3 trial in Chinese men reportedly did not separate from placebo.[2]

angle.text: Pyrilutamide is applied to the scalp to reduce androgen signalling in hair follicles. Company-reported trials show hair count gains versus baseline, while results against placebo are mixed, and it remains investigational.
